misconceptions.statement: Feeling sad, angry or scared is bad, and good people only feel happy.
misconceptions.why: Children are often praised for being cheerful and scolded for showing anger or sadness.
misconceptions.fix: All emotions, including sadness, anger and fear, are natural and everyone feels them. What matters is how we handle them.

probe.question: Riya feels very sad after losing a match. Is something wrong with her for feeling this way?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a good person should not feel sad.

misconceptions.root_belief: some natural feelings are bad and must not exist

misconceptions.statement: Boys should not cry or show feelings because it is a sign of weakness.
misconceptions.why: Social messages like 'be a man' teach children that showing emotion is shameful.
misconceptions.fix: Crying and showing feelings are normal human reactions for everyone. Letting feelings out is healthy, not weak.

probe.question: Arjun cries when he fails a test. What does this say about him?
probe.wrong_answer: That he is weak.

misconceptions.root_belief: gender decides how a person may feel
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on gender stereotypes and emotional expression in adolescents

misconceptions.statement: The best way to deal with a worry is to keep it inside and not think about it.
misconceptions.why: Ignoring a problem gives short relief, so it seems to work.
misconceptions.fix: Bottled-up feelings usually grow stronger. Talking, writing or drawing about them helps them settle.

probe.question: Meena is upset about a fight with a friend. What is the best way to deal with it?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep quiet and forget about it.

misconceptions.root_belief: hiding a problem makes it go away
misconceptions.source_hint: research on emotional suppression and avoidance coping

misconceptions.statement: All stress is harmful and should be completely avoided.
misconceptions.why: The word 'stress' is mostly used in a negative way in daily talk.
misconceptions.fix: A small amount of stress can help us stay alert and prepare, such as before a race. It becomes a problem when it is too much or lasts too long.

probe.question: Is a little nervous energy before a school performance always bad?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, all stress is bad.

misconceptions.root_belief: a thing is either wholly good or wholly bad

misconceptions.statement: Children do not get real stress because they have no responsibilities.
misconceptions.why: Adults' problems like jobs and money are more visible than children's worries.
misconceptions.fix: Children and teenagers also feel stress from exams, friends, family and changes. It is real and deserves attention.

probe.question: Can a Class 8 student feel serious stress?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only grown-ups with jobs get stress.

misconceptions.root_belief: only grown-ups have serious problems

misconceptions.statement: Sleeping less and studying all night is the best way to do well in exams.
misconceptions.why: Students think more hours of study always means more marks.
misconceptions.fix: The brain needs sleep to remember and think clearly. Regular sleep, breaks and exercise help performance and lower stress.

probe.question: Before an exam, Ravi studies the whole night without sleep. Is this a good plan?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more study hours always give better marks.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: sleep research on memory and adolescent exam performance

misconceptions.statement: Feeling anxious or nervous means a person has a mental illness.
misconceptions.why: Students take one common feeling as proof of a disease.
misconceptions.fix: Everyone feels anxious sometimes. It becomes an anxiety problem only when it is very strong, lasts long and disturbs daily life.

probe.question: Sana feels nervous before an exam. Does she have an anxiety disorder?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, being nervous means she has a mental illness.

misconceptions.root_belief: one sign means the whole condition

misconceptions.statement: Anxiety is just silliness, and a person can stop it by trying harder.
misconceptions.why: Anxiety cannot be seen, so people think it is only a matter of attitude.
misconceptions.fix: Anxiety is a real condition linked to the brain and body, and strong willpower alone cannot switch it off. Support and sometimes treatment help.

probe.question: A friend has constant strong anxiety. What should they do to stop it?
probe.wrong_answer: Just try harder and stop being silly.

misconceptions.root_belief: feelings can be switched off by will alone
misconceptions.source_hint: mental health literacy surveys on stigma toward anxiety

misconceptions.statement: Anxiety is only in the mind and never causes body symptoms.
misconceptions.why: Students separate the mind and the body completely.
misconceptions.fix: Anxiety can cause a fast heartbeat, sweating, stomach ache, headache and trouble sleeping.

probe.question: Before a test Kabir gets a stomach ache and a racing heart. Can anxiety cause this?
probe.wrong_answer: No, anxiety only affects thoughts.

misconceptions.root_belief: mind and body are separate
misconceptions.source_hint: research on somatic symptoms in child and adolescent anxiety

misconceptions.statement: Your marks show how valuable you are as a person.
misconceptions.why: Praise and comparison at home and school focus mainly on marks.
misconceptions.fix: Marks show how you did in one test. They do not measure your worth, kindness, talents or future.

probe.question: Neha got low marks in maths. Does it mean she is not a valuable person?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, low marks mean she is worth less.

misconceptions.root_belief: one number measures a whole person
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on academic contingent self-worth in Indian adolescents

misconceptions.statement: The more pressure we feel before exams, the better we will perform.
misconceptions.why: Some pressure does push students to work, so they assume more is always better.
misconceptions.fix: Moderate pressure can motivate, but too much pressure causes panic and blocks memory and thinking.

probe.question: Will extreme pressure from everyone before the exam improve a student's score?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, more pressure gives better marks.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on arousal and performance in test anxiety

misconceptions.statement: Failing one exam ruins your whole life.
misconceptions.why: Adults and peers often talk about one board exam as the only chance.
misconceptions.fix: One exam is a single step. There are many chances and paths to try again and succeed.

probe.question: A student fails a unit test. Is their future finished?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, one failure ruins everything.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event decides everything forever

misconceptions.statement: Taking breaks or playing during exam days is wasting time.
misconceptions.why: Students link only continuous study with seriousness.
misconceptions.fix: Short breaks, play and rest refresh the brain and improve learning. A simple timetable with breaks reduces stress.

probe.question: Is a 20 minute walk during study time a waste?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it wastes study time.

misconceptions.root_belief: continuous effort always beats rest

misconceptions.statement: Mental health and mental illness mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Both phrases contain 'mental' and are often used together.
misconceptions.fix: Mental health is our state of emotional and thinking well-being, which everyone has. Mental illness is a condition that affects it and can be treated.

probe.question: A student says 'I am working on my mental health.' Does this mean they are mentally ill?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, mental health means illness.

misconceptions.root_belief: related words mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: mental health literacy research on terminology confusion

misconceptions.statement: Mental health matters only for people who are already ill.
misconceptions.why: People talk about physical health only when someone falls sick.
misconceptions.fix: Like physical health, mental health needs care for everyone every day, through sleep, friends, activity and talking.

probe.question: Does a healthy, happy student need to care for their mental health?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only ill people need it.

misconceptions.root_belief: health matters only when sick

misconceptions.statement: Having a mental illness is a sign of weakness or a character flaw.
misconceptions.why: Society treats strength as never struggling.
misconceptions.fix: Mental illness is a health condition, not a weakness. It can happen to anyone, just like diabetes or asthma.

probe.question: Why does a person get depression?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are weak-minded.

misconceptions.root_belief: strength means never struggling
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO and surveys of stigma toward mental illness

misconceptions.statement: People with mental illness are dangerous or 'mad'.
misconceptions.why: Films and news often show them as violent.
misconceptions.fix: Most people with mental illness are not dangerous. They are more likely to be hurt or left out than to hurt others.

probe.question: Should we stay away from a classmate who has anxiety?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they may be dangerous.

misconceptions.root_belief: what looks different is a threat
misconceptions.source_hint: media portrayal studies of mental illness

misconceptions.statement: Mental illness never gets better, so treatment is useless.
misconceptions.why: Students think a long-lasting problem is permanent.
misconceptions.fix: Most mental health problems can be treated with talk therapy, medicines or both, and many people recover and lead full lives.

probe.question: Can a person with depression get better?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it never goes away.

misconceptions.root_belief: a long-lasting problem is permanent
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO mental health fact sheets on treatability

misconceptions.statement: Positive thinking alone can cure any mental illness, so no treatment is needed.
misconceptions.why: Motivational messages say a good attitude fixes everything.
misconceptions.fix: Being positive helps, but real conditions often need support from counsellors or doctors, just like a fever needs care.

probe.question: A friend has severe depression. Is positive thinking alone enough?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, just think positive.

misconceptions.root_belief: positive thinking alone fixes any problem

misconceptions.statement: Mental illness is caused by black magic, evil spirits or punishment for bad deeds.
misconceptions.why: Traditional beliefs explain unseen problems with unseen forces.
misconceptions.fix: Mental illness comes from a mix of brain chemistry, genes, life events and stress, not from magic or punishment. Doctors can help.

probe.question: A man hears voices and feels very low. What is the likely cause?
probe.wrong_answer: An evil spirit or a curse.

misconceptions.root_belief: unseen causes explain what we cannot see
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of supernatural beliefs about mental illness in India

misconceptions.statement: Talking about my problems will only make them worse or burden others.
misconceptions.why: Students fear being judged or being a nuisance.
misconceptions.fix: Sharing with a trusted adult usually brings relief and ideas for solving the problem. Most adults want to help.

probe.question: Tara is worried about bullying. Should she tell her teacher?
probe.wrong_answer: No, talking will make it worse.

misconceptions.root_belief: speaking about a problem makes it bigger

misconceptions.statement: Only parents can be trusted adults.
misconceptions.why: Children think of help as coming only from home.
misconceptions.fix: A trusted adult can be a parent, relative, teacher, school counsellor or any adult who listens and keeps you safe.

probe.question: If a student cannot talk to parents, who else can they go to?
probe.wrong_answer: No one, only parents can help.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one kind of person can help

misconceptions.statement: Only people who are 'mad' or in extreme crisis go to a counsellor or doctor.
misconceptions.why: Seeking help is linked with shame in many communities.
misconceptions.fix: Anyone can meet a counsellor for stress, worry or sadness. Going early is a wise step, like seeing a doctor for a fever.

probe.question: Aman feels very stressed but not in crisis. Should he see a counsellor?
probe.wrong_answer: No, counsellors are only for very serious cases.

misconceptions.root_belief: seek help only when it is extreme
misconceptions.source_hint: surveys on help-seeking barriers among Indian adolescents

misconceptions.statement: Mental health helplines are only for adults and cost money.
misconceptions.why: Students assume services are meant for others and are paid.
misconceptions.fix: Free helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) run by the Government of India offer support round the clock, and young people can call too.

probe.question: Can a Class 9 student call Tele-MANAS 14416 for support?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is for adults and is paid.

misconceptions.root_belief: services are meant for others, not me

misconceptions.statement: If a friend shares their sadness, I must keep it a secret even if they might be in danger.
misconceptions.why: Loyalty is understood as never telling anyone.
misconceptions.fix: If a friend seems to be in danger or may hurt themselves, tell a trusted adult. This is caring, not betrayal.

probe.question: A friend says they feel hopeless and want to hurt themselves, but asks you to keep quiet. What do you do?
probe.wrong_answer: Keep the secret and tell no one.

misconceptions.root_belief: loyalty means never telling anyone

misconceptions.statement: Asking a friend if they feel very low or hopeless will put harmful ideas in their head.
misconceptions.why: People fear that naming a danger creates it.
misconceptions.fix: Asking kindly and listening does not cause harm and often brings relief. Then help them reach a trusted adult.

probe.question: Should you ask a withdrawn friend, 'Are you okay?'
probe.wrong_answer: No, asking may make things worse.

misconceptions.root_belief: naming a danger creates the danger
misconceptions.source_hint: WHO guidance and studies on asking about suicidal thoughts
